name: Italian Baroque

revival_periods.note: The Baroque scenographic plan and giant coupled order return through the Ecole des Beaux-Arts and the City Beautiful movement, applied to stations, museums and civic centres.

lineage.note: Unbroken workshop and treatise transmission through Michelangelo, Vignola and the Mannerists. Vignola's Regola of 1562 remains the working manual; the orders themselves are not renegotiated.

The Baroque wall is the precise inversion of the Palladian one: curved where Palladio is planar, accelerating where he is even, multi-planar in column projection where he keeps one plane, and broken in its pediments where he keeps them whole.
Imperial scale and the ceremonial axis are quoted directly - Bernini's colonnade is a Roman forum portico deployed for papal ceremony - but the structural means are masonry and stucco, not concrete.

description.short: The classical order retained intact while the wall it governs is bent, layered and accelerated, producing an architecture of continuous surface and controlled emotional effect.
description.long:
The Baroque is often described as classicism gone loose, which gets it exactly backwards. Borromini's mouldings are more precise than Bramante's, not less; the module is preserved to the millimetre. What changes is what the module is applied to. In the Renaissance the wall is a flat plane and the orders are a grid laid on it. In the Baroque the wall itself becomes a deformable surface - convex here, concave there, its plan generated by interlocking ovals, circles and triangles - and the orders are made to follow it around the curve. A single bay may contain a pilaster, a half-column, a three-quarter column and a free-standing column, each in a different plane, so that the facade is read as depth rather than as pattern. The building stops being a figure you look at and becomes a space you are inside of even when you are outdoors.

The conditions are Counter-Reformation and papal. The Council of Trent closed in 1563 having decided, against the Protestant position, that images, ceremony and sensory persuasion were legitimate instruments of faith. That is a design brief. The new orders - Jesuits, Oratorians, Theatines - needed churches for large congregations focused on preaching and on the sacrament, which means a single wide nave with side chapels rather than aisles, an unobstructed sightline to the altar, and a dome over the crossing to concentrate light exactly where the mystery happens. Papal Rome simultaneously had a city-planning problem: pilgrim routes between the seven basilicas, needing obelisks, fountains, straightened streets and axial termini. Sixtus V's replanning from 1585 is the point at which architecture starts designing the space between buildings, and this is arguably the Baroque's most durable export - it is what Haussmann, L'Enfant and the City Beautiful all inherit.

What it reacts against, within its own family, is the terminal stasis of High Renaissance and Palladian composition. A Palladian front is resolved and finished; there is nowhere for the eye to go, which is the point. The Baroque decides that resolution is a waste of the observer's attention, and organises everything as movement toward a climax: bays compress and columns multiply as they approach the axis, entablatures break forward over the centre, the pediment splits open to admit a sculptural event, and the composition finishes on the sky with a silhouette of figures rather than a cornice line.

Inside San Carlo alle Quattro Fontane, on a corner site of about twenty by twelve metres, the experience is disorienting in a way you cannot immediately explain. The lower order is a continuous undulating colonnade with no flat wall anywhere; the entablature above it runs unbroken around every curve like a taut band; and then the coffered oval dome above appears to hang free, lit from a lantern you cannot quite see, its interlocking crosses, hexagons and octagons diminishing so aggressively that the dome reads as twice its true height. Nothing is applied. The geometry goes all the way through the building, and the sensation is of standing inside a solved equation that is still moving.

defining_characteristics: The wall treated as a continuous deformable surface, curved in plan, with the orders following it around convex and concave sweeps
Multiple planes of column projection within a single bay (pilaster, half, three-quarter, free-standing) to produce read depth
A rhythm that accelerates toward the axis - bays compress and articulation multiplies at the centre
Plan geometry generated from interlocking ovals, circles and triangles rather than from additive rectangular bays
Broken, segmental and scrolled pediments used as compositional openings for sculpture or light
Concealed and directed light: hidden lanterns, windows behind cornices, and openings sized to create a single dramatic gradient
The building composed with its urban void - piazza, obelisk, fountain and street axis designed as one work
diagnostic_tells: A facade whose plan line is curved - if you can see the wall bend, no earlier classical style will account for it
Entablature that breaks forward and back over each change of column plane rather than running as a single straight band
Giant order of two-plus storeys with a small subordinate order tucked beneath it in the same bay
Pediments split at the apex, or a segmental pediment nested inside a triangular one
The silhouette against the sky is populated - statues, urns, volutes, scrolled buttresses - rather than terminated by a horizontal cornice

distinguished_from.difference: Flat versus curved wall; even versus accelerating bay rhythm; single versus multiple planes of column projection; whole versus broken pediments; horizontal cornice termination versus a populated sky silhouette.

The French keep the wall flat and get their plasticity by projecting whole masses - pavilions and avant-corps - forward as blocks. If the plasticity comes from a curved wall surface it is Italian; if it comes from rectangular blocks stepping forward, it is French.

The Spanish variant concentrates all ornament into a dense retablo-like frontispiece surrounded by plain wall, and does not curve the wall in plan. Italian Baroque distributes plasticity across the whole surface.

proportional_system.governing_logic: The order is retained exactly as Vignola codified it (module = half the lower diameter, in 12 or 18 parts), but the governing geometry of the whole moves from the additive bay to a continuous figure - interlocking ovals, circles and equilateral triangles set out on the plan and then extruded as curved wall surface. Proportion is dynamic: the module stays fixed while the surface it governs deforms.
typical_ratios: Oval domes and plans with major:minor axis typically 3:2 to 5:3
San Carlo alle Quattro Fontane: plan traditionally analysed as two equilateral triangles on a shared base, with circles inscribed, within an oval - on a site of roughly 20 x 12 m
Giant order spanning two storeys, entablature 1/5 to 1/4 of column height, with a subordinate small order of about 0.4 the giant order's height
Column projection graded in four planes across a half-bay, each step 1/2 to 1 module
Church front width:height approximately 1:1 for the two-storey scheme, with the upper storey 0.6 to 0.7 the width of the lower and joined by volutes
Nave width:height typically 1:2 to 1:2.5; side chapel openings 1/2 to 2/3 of the nave bay width
Dome coffering diminishing 15 to 25 percent per ring to exaggerate apparent height
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Accelerating toward the centre: A-B-C-B-A, where C is narrower than B and B narrower than A, and where the density of articulation increases inversely with bay width. The entablature breaks forward at each escalation, so the horizontal reads as a sequence of steps rather than as a line.

massing_affinities.note: The Roman palazzo persists as the domestic and institutional type; the Baroque changes its face and its stair, not its skeleton.
Suburban villas and casini open a cour d'honneur toward the approach, which the Baroque then treats as a stage set.
Baroque Rome and Turin build long uniform street walls with a single palazzo swelling out of them at the axis.
Used, but with the pediment broken and the wings curved forward as quadrant colonnades rather than kept straight.

Baroque irregularity is always resolved about an axis. Irregularity for its own sake, composed for a moving viewpoint without a governing symmetry, belongs to the picturesque and is a different argument entirely.

constraints.statement: If the wall curves in plan, the entablature must curve with it as a continuous member; a straight entablature over a curved wall is a hard error.

Column projection must increase monotonically toward the axis within a bay - pilaster, then half, then three-quarter, then free-standing. Random alternation of planes is not Baroque layering, it is noise.
Bay widths must narrow toward the centre by 10 to 25 percent per step. An even bay rhythm with Baroque ornament applied is Mannerist or revivalist, not Baroque.

Oval and curved-wall plans require masonry or reinforced construction with wall thickness of at least 1/10 the clear span; the geometry is not achievable in light frame without losing the depth of reveal that makes it read.

test.note: Combines a section reading (wall_thickness_in) with a plan reading (room_clear_span_ft, converted to inches) to test the 1/10-of-span slenderness floor. 'Not achievable in light frame without losing the depth of reveal' is prose commentary on the same rule, not a second fact.

constraints.statement: Broken pediments must be broken FOR something - a cartouche, a statue, a window admitting light. An empty break is a decorative tic, not a Baroque device.

exemplars.name: San Carlo alle Quattro Fontane
exemplars.note: Borromini; church built 1638-1641, dedicated 1646; facade begun in Borromini's last years and the upper stage completed after his death in 1667. The undulating wall and interlocking-geometry oval dome in their purest form.
exemplars.why: Roma Capitale's record states three of this node's own diagnostic tells in its own words -- the serpentine facade, the entablature flexing round the whole perimeter, and the elliptical coffered dome whose coffers diminish upward -- while pointing out that the church is 'often unjustely forgotten' beside the larger Baroque churches.

exemplars.name: Sant'Ivo alla Sapienza
exemplars.note: Borromini, 1642-1660. Plan generated from two superimposed equilateral triangles; concave courtyard front and a spiral lantern.
exemplars.why: Roma Capitale's Italian record says the centralised plan draws 'una sorta di stella a sei punte' and that the walls follow its perimeter, which is the node's two-superimposed-triangles claim stated by a register; that same page calls the church the work of 'il geniale Francesco Borromini' and 'un capolavoro dallo straordinario valore artistico e tecnico'.

exemplars.name: Sant'Andrea al Quirinale
exemplars.note: Bernini, 1658-1670. Transverse oval plan with the entrance on the short axis - the compression of the approach is the whole design.
exemplars.why: Roma Capitale's record says Bernini 'considered it his best work for the perfect balance between architecture, sculpture and painting' and independently states the transverse oval -- 'the major axis perpendicular to the entrance' -- that this node reads as the whole design.

exemplars.name: Piazza San Pietro colonnade
exemplars.note: Bernini, 1656-1667. Two quadrant colonnades of four ranks of Tuscan columns; architecture used to shape an urban void rather than an enclosure.
exemplars.why: The Holy See's own record states the colonnade as 284 columns and 88 piers in four ranks under 140 statues, which is the one place in this cluster where a register supplies enough numbers to check a claim -- and where two Vatican sources disagree by three metres about the height of the columns.

exemplars.name: Palazzo Carignano
exemplars.note: Commissioned from Guarino Guarini in 1679 by Emanuele Filiberto di Savoia-Carignano, who according to the Residenze Reali Sabaude took Bernini's Louvre designs as the model. Undulating brick front; monumental oval atrium with two symmetrical ceremonial stairs; originally a C-shaped plan open toward the gardens.
exemplars.why: The Residenze Reali Sabaude call it 'una delle piu originali costruzioni del barocco' and single out the curving line of the brick facade; the node's geography names Piedmont and every other exemplar it carried was in Rome or the Vatican.

exemplars.name: Late Baroque Towns of the Val di Noto
exemplars.note: Eight towns rebuilt after the earthquake of 1693 -- Caltagirone, Militello Val di Catania, Catania, Modica, Noto, Palazzolo Acreide, Ragusa and Scicli. Not one building: the record is the World Heritage listing, and what it documents is a rebuilding programme across eight town plans.
exemplars.why: UNESCO's criterion (ii) calls these towns 'the culmination and final flowering of Baroque art in Europe' and its authenticity statement points at the almost completely preserved town plans -- which is the node's own claim that the Baroque's most durable export was the design of the space between buildings, and its geography named Sicily with nothing to show for it.

sources: Rudolf Wittkower, Art and Architecture in Italy 1600-1750, Pelican History of Art
Paolo Portoghesi, The Rome of Borromini: Architecture as Language (1968)
Giacomo Barozzi da Vignola, Regola delli cinque ordini d'architettura (1562)

proportion_packs.note: Judgment binding: italian-baroque is not in vignola-composite's own applies_to. Bound anyway because this style's own proportional_system states the order 'is retained exactly as Vignola codified it' while only the wall around it deforms -- module fixed, surface dynamic. Composite is the richest of the five and the natural register for the giant order at San Carlo alle Quattro Fontane and Sant'Andrea al Quirinale, matching the brief's own steer toward a richer, more ornamented order for this style.

Judgment binding. Named directly: the Piazza San Pietro colonnade is 'two quadrant colonnades of four ranks of Tuscan columns' in this style's own exemplar note. Bernini's Doric-plain register for shaping urban void rather than enclosing a room.

Judgment binding. An alternate giant-order register, less ornate than Composite, for the church and palazzo fronts where the sculptural intensity is carried by broken pediments and multi-plane column projection (c02) rather than by the capital itself.

Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to. Wittkower's own study, which is room-harmonic's authority, is substantially a study of Italian High Renaissance and Baroque interiors, so the fit is closer here than the pack's Palladian phrasing suggests -- though it governs the individual room, not the oval, triangle-and-circle plan geometry that generates the whole building, which is outside anything a room-proportion pack in this library models.
